soul.hero_subtitle: Stories, languages and traditions of Benin, told with the people who carry them.
soul.hero_note: This section is under construction: every story, translation and recording will be validated by qualified people before being presented as final.

heritage.title: Heritage stories
heritage.intro: Every site has a story that unfolds over time. Pick a place, then walk through its timeline.

abomey.intro: Capital of the Kingdom of Dahomey, Abomey preserves the palaces of a dynasty of twelve kings. The bas-reliefs on its walls kept the memory of reigns and key events.
abomey.source: UNESCO, Royal Palaces of Abomey (inscribed in 1985); Historical Museum of Abomey.

events.title: A dynasty of twelve kings
events.text: According to UNESCO, twelve kings succeeded one another at the head of the Kingdom of Dahomey. Each added his own palace within the royal enclosure of Abomey.

events.title: Access to the coast
events.text: Under King Agadja, Dahomey conquered Allada, then Ouidah in 1727. The kingdom thus gained access to the coast and to Atlantic trade, including the slave trade.

events.title: The reign of Guézo
events.text: Guézo's reign was one of the longest of the dynasty. Dahomey was then a powerful and highly organised state.

events.title: The Franco-Dahomean War
events.text: The war ended with the surrender of King Béhanzin, who was exiled to Martinique and then Algeria. The kingdom came under French colonial rule.

events.title: World Heritage
events.text: The Royal Palaces of Abomey are inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List.

events.title: The return of the royal treasures
events.text: France returns to Benin twenty-six works from the royal treasures of Abomey, taken during the 1892 conquest.

ouidah.intro: A former port of the Atlantic slave trade and a central place of vodun traditions, Ouidah is today a place of memory and living practice. The Slave Route, about four kilometres long, leads to the Door of No Return, facing the ocean.
ouidah.source: UNESCO, The Slave Route project; Ouidah History Museum.

events.title: The Portuguese fort
events.text: Portugal founds the fort of São João Baptista de Ajudá in Ouidah. It now houses the Ouidah History Museum.

events.title: The Dahomean conquest
events.text: Dahomey conquers Ouidah. The port is then one of the main embarkation points for captives bound for the Americas.

events.title: The Slave Route
events.text: UNESCO's The Slave Route project is launched in Ouidah, to raise awareness of the history of the slave trade and its consequences.

events.title: A recognised religion
events.text: Vodun is officially recognised in Benin. January 10 becomes a public holiday dedicated to indigenous religions.

portonovo.intro: The official capital of Benin, Porto-Novo is the former capital of the Kingdom of Hogbonou. Its heritage blends royal traditions, Afro-Brazilian influences and colonial legacy.
portonovo.source: Honmè Museum (former royal palace). Sources to be completed with the museum and heritage services.

events.title: The Kingdom of Hogbonou
events.text: The kingdom develops along the lagoon. Portuguese merchants give the town the name “Porto-Novo”.

events.title: The protectorate
events.text: King Sodji accepts a French protectorate over his kingdom.

events.title: A quiet capital
events.text: Porto-Novo is the official capital of the country, while Cotonou concentrates the government and economic activity. The Honmè Palace, a former royal residence, houses a museum.

stories.title: Cultural stories
stories.intro: From kingdoms to know-how, explore Benin's traditions chapter by chapter.
stories.review: Provisional text: this content must be reviewed and completed with practitioners, religious leaders and specialists before final publication.
respect: Ask permission before photographing or filming a ceremony or a person.
Some places and rites are reserved for initiates: respect the restrictions.
Go with a trusted local guide.
A ceremony is not a show: you are not merely a spectator.

cards.title: Historic kingdoms
cards.summary: From the coast to the north, several kingdoms shaped present-day Benin.

chapters.title: Allada, Abomey, Porto-Novo
chapters.text: According to many traditions, the royal families of Allada, Dahomey and Hogbonou (Porto-Novo) share a common origin, linked to the Aja people who came from the Tado region.

chapters.title: Kétou
chapters.text: Kétou is a former Yoruba kingdom. It is one of the centres of the Gelede tradition.

chapters.title: Nikki and the Borgou
chapters.text: In the north, the Bariba kingdom of Nikki shaped the Borgou region. The Gaani festival, held every year in Nikki, keeps its memory alive.

cards.title: The arts
cards.summary: On walls, on cloth, behind masks: history is told in images.

chapters.title: The bas-reliefs of Abomey
chapters.text: The palace walls are decorated with coloured earth bas-reliefs. Each motif evokes a ruler, an emblem animal or a key event.

chapters.title: Appliqué textiles
chapters.text: Appliqués are cloths decorated with cut-out motifs that are then sewn on. In Abomey, they celebrate the emblems of the kings.

chapters.title: The Gelede
chapters.text: Inscribed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage, the Gelede are mask performances that honour mothers and their spiritual power. They combine dance, song and sculpture.

cards.title: Traditional festivals
cards.summary: Moments when a whole community comes together.

chapters.title: January 10
chapters.text: Every year, the festival of indigenous religions, or vodun festival, gathers practitioners and visitors, notably in Ouidah.

chapters.title: The Gaani
chapters.text: The Gaani is the great festival of the Bariba people in Nikki. It includes ceremonies and horse parades.

chapters.title: Taking part with respect
chapters.text: A festival is not a show put on for visitors. Ask a local guide, ask before filming and follow the organisers' instructions.

cards.title: Know-how
cards.summary: Skills passed down from generation to generation.

chapters.title: Metal
chapters.text: Lost-wax bronze and brass work is practised in several regions. The object is first modelled in wax, then covered in clay before the metal is poured.

chapters.title: Textiles
chapters.text: Weaving, dyeing and appliqué carry meaningful patterns. Each workshop has its own codes.

chapters.title: Clay and fibre
chapters.text: Pottery and basketry are part of daily life: holding water, storing, carrying. These skills are often passed down from generation to generation.

cards.title: Vodun
cards.summary: A living religion, to be approached with listening and respect.

chapters.title: A religion, not folklore
chapters.text: Vodun is a religion practised in Benin, Togo and the wider region. It organises the relationship between humans, ancestors and the forces of nature.

chapters.title: A world of deities
chapters.text: In Fon cosmology, Mawu and Lisa are associated with creation, and many vodun watch over specific domains. Legba is regarded as the intermediary between humans and the deities.

chapters.title: A link with the diaspora
chapters.text: Practices from West Africa took on their own forms in Haiti, Cuba and Brazil, for example Haitian Vodou or Candomblé.
